notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Nehemiah 9, based on the sources available from the permitted sites.

---

## Nehemiah 9 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview (v. 1–38)

The chapter records a great national fast and confession, two days after the Feast of Tabernacles (the 24th day of Tisri). The Levites lead a long prayer — often called the longest prayer in the Bible — surveying God's faithfulness from creation through the conquest, confessing Israel's repeated rebellion, and pleading for present deliverance. The prayer is one of three great national confessions in the OT (alongside Ezra 9 and Daniel 9).

- Precept Austin notes this is "one of the great prayers of confession in the Bible…full of rich instruction about who God is, who we are, and how God has graciously worked on behalf of His people." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-9-commentary
- The chapter is closely united with Nehemiah 10, where the sealed covenant is recorded. — Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/nehemiah-9.html

---

### v. 1 — The assembly of humble repentance

The people gathered on the 24th day of the seventh month (Tisri), two days after the Feast of Tabernacles ended (cf. Lev. 23:34–39). They came with fasting, sackcloth (coarse fabric), and dust on their heads — all traditional signs of deep mourning and self-humiliation.

- **Gill**: These were "outward tokens of mourning and humiliation" that could not be shown during the festival itself; now that the feast was over, they returned to the penitent spirit first seen in Nehemiah 8:9. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "After one day of rest, the people assembled with all the tokens of sorrow, even to dust on the head (1 Samuel 4:12): the external signs and the internal spirit were one." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Enduring Word (David Guzik)**: Fasting showed "their lowly, humble state…they considered themselves so poor before God that they took no food." Sackcloth and dust said "we are so troubled by our sin that the normal comforts of life are unimportant." He adds that this humble repentance came *after* great victories — the wall was complete and the people had obeyed God's word — showing that "repentance isn't something we finish after coming to Jesus. It is something that grows as we grow closer to Jesus." Quoting Spurgeon: "Repentance grows as faith grows…it is the grace of a lifetime, like faith itself." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/
- **Bob Utley (Precept Austin)**: Notes that the repentant actions were characteristic of the Day of Atonement (the 10th day), occurring here 14 days later. He observes that during the reading of the law the returnees had already felt "remorse and guilt" (cf. Neh. 8:9). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-9-commentary

---

### v. 2 — Separation from foreigners and confession of sins

Those of Israelite descent ("the seed of Israel") separated themselves from all foreigners (literally "strangers"), then stood and confessed both their own sins and the iniquities of their fathers.

- **Gill**: The "seed of Israel" were "genuine Israelites, of the seed of Abraham," and the separation likely involved those who had married foreign wives — a sign of true repentance. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "The change to 'seed' has here a deep propriety. They carefully avoided the many aliens among them throughout this fast." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Believer's Study Bible (via Precept Austin)**: "In neither instance does pride motivate the separation, but rather concern for the reestablishment of covenant relationship." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-9-commentary
- **Enduring Word**: Regarding confessing "the iniquities of their fathers," Guzik clarifies this does not mean "some type of 'generational curse' that had to be broken. God does not punish the children for their father's sin, and it is evil to say He does (Ezekiel 18)." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/
- **James Boice (via Precept Austin)**: Points out that confessing the sins of their fathers was "the opposite of what most people do today. Today, if people refer to the sins of their parents at all, it is to excuse themselves by blaming their parents, rather than to confess and mourn over the sins of their parents." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-9-commentary

---

### v. 3 — Reading the law and worship for a quarter-day each

They stood and read from the Book of the Law for a quarter of the day (~3 hours, likely 6–9 a.m.), then for another quarter (~9 a.m.–noon) they confessed and worshipped.

- **Gill**: Locates them in the outer court of the temple; the reading occupied from sunrise to the morning sacrifice (~9 a.m.), and confession/worship from then until noon. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "Both day and night were divided into four parts. All orders standing in their respective place, the reading occupied the morning and the worship the afternoon." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Derek Kidner (via Enduring Word)**: "In the light of the previous chapter we may take it that the reading was no mere stream of words, but punctuated with explanatory comments and applications to the present situation." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/
- **Smith's Writings (via StudyLight)**: "The return to the word of God resulted first in the people rendering to the Lord His portion…The second result is seen in this chapter in which the people take their true place before God." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hsw/nehemiah-9.html

---

### v. 4 — The first group of Levites cries out to God

Eight Levites (Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani) stood on the raised platform ("the stairs of the Levites") and cried out with a loud voice to the LORD.

- **Ellicott**: The "stairs of the Levites" refers to "the scaffold of the Levites…the steps of ascent to the pulpit of Ezra (Nehemiah 8:2)." He notes these eight Levites "offered a prayer which is not inserted" — they cried out, but the actual recorded prayer comes from the second group in v. 5. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Gill**: The "stairs" was "an elevated place where the Levites used to stand when they sang at the time of sacrifice, and where they might be seen and heard by the people." They "cried with a loud voice…praying with great fervency, and making bitter lamentation for the sins of the people and their own." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Enduring Word**: "Obviously, all eight of these men did not pray the following prayer at the same time. Perhaps it was written out and they took turns, perhaps it was spontaneously prayed in succession, or perhaps (and according to tradition), Ezra prayed this prayer." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/

---

### v. 5 — The second group of Levites calls the people to bless God

A slightly different list of Levites (Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah) said, "Stand up and bless the LORD your God from everlasting to everlasting."

- **Ellicott**: The LXX (Septuagint) "arbitrarily omit all names after Kadmiel. Similarly, they insert 'and Ezra said' before Nehemiah 9:6. The psalm was perhaps composed by Ezra, but uttered by the Levites in the name of the congregation." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Gill**: The command to "stand up" suggests that though they were already standing (v. 2–3), "through shame and confusion of face, and awe of the Divine Majesty, might be fallen on their faces to the ground." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Layman's Bible Commentary**: Notes that either the editor used two sources with two different lists, or "two different stages in the ceremonies involved different groups with some duplication." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/nehemiah-9.html

---

### v. 6 — Praise to God the Creator and Preserver

"You alone are the LORD. You created the heavens, the highest heavens…You give life to all things, and the host of heaven worships You."

- **Gill**: "Thou, even thou art Lord alone" — "whose name alone is Jehovah, the one only true and living God." On "thou preservest them all," Gill cross-references Hebrews 1:3, noting that all things "consist in thee, and are upheld in their being by thee." The "host of heaven" includes the angels primarily (cf. Heb. 1:6), not merely the stars. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "Preservest them all.—In this comprehensiveness reproduced only in Hebrews 1:3. The host of heaven.—First the stars, but here the angels (Psalm 103:21)." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm

---

### v. 7 — God chose Abram and brought him from Ur

"You are the LORD, the God who chose Abram, who brought him out of Ur of the Chaldeans and gave him the name Abraham."

- **Gill**: Notes that Ur was possibly "the sacred fire, which the Chaldeans worshipped," and that God chose Abram from among them. The name change to Abraham came with the covenant of circumcision (Gen. 17:5). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Precept Austin (Steven Cole)**: "God chose Abram, brought him out from Ur of the Chaldees, and gave him the name Abraham (9:7; the only Old Testament reference outside of Genesis to God's changing Abram's name)." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-9-commentary

---

### v. 8 — God found Abraham faithful and made the covenant

"You found his heart faithful before You, and made a covenant with him to give the land…You have kept Your promise, because You are righteous."

- **Gill**: "A true believer in his word and promises, Genesis 15:6…as abundantly appeared in the trial of him, in offering up his son, Genesis 22:1." The covenant was made "not to him personally, but to his posterity." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: The Hivites are "for some reason omitted" from the list of Canaanite nations. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm

---

### vv. 9–11 — The Exodus: affliction seen, the sea divided, pursuers destroyed

- **Gill**: God "was not a mere spectator" of the affliction in Egypt, "but looked upon them in it with pity and compassion." On v. 11, the Egyptians were thrown "with great ease, and with indignation…as a stone into the mighty waters; where they sunk and perished." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: On v. 11, he notes that the phrasing recalls the Song of Moses (Ex. 15), with deliberate "identity and variation" in the Hebrew. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm

---

### v. 12 — The pillar of cloud and fire

"You led them with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way."

- **Gill**: The cloud sheltered them "from the heat of the sun in a dry and barren wilderness"; the fire gave light "through a trackless desert." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html

---

### vv. 13–14 — Sinai, the Law, and the Sabbath

"You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven. You gave them just ordinances, true laws, and good statutes…You revealed to them Your holy Sabbath."

- **Gill**: God came down "by some visible tokens of his presence, as a cloud, fire, smoke, etc. which must be understood consistent with his omniscience." The Sabbath was "not made known to others, and was peculiar to the Jewish nation, and a privilege granted to them, to have rest corporeal and spiritual, typical of the rest in Christ." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "Right judgements.—Five of the names given to the law of God in Psalms 119 are singled out and applied to the Sinaitic legislation…But the emphasis here is on the adjectives 'right,' 'true,' 'good,' as belonging rather to the eternal principles of the Decalogue." On v. 14: "Every word here, as well as the prominence given to this among the other 'commandments,' must be noted as illustrating the importance of this ordinance in the covenant of chapter 10 and throughout the book." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm

---

### v. 15 — Manna, water from the rock, and the promise of the land

"In their hunger You gave them bread from heaven; in their thirst You brought them water from the rock. You told them to go in and possess the land."

- **Gill**: The manna satisfied hunger (Ex. 16:3), the water was given both soon after leaving Egypt and just before entering Canaan (Ex. 17:6; Num. 20:11), and the promise was made "to them and to their fathers also." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "Bread from heaven.—A change of phrase, which our Lord consecrated for ever (John 6)." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm

---

### vv. 16–17a — Israel's arrogant response: stiff-necked rebellion

"But they and our fathers became arrogant and stiff-necked…They stiffened their necks and appointed a leader to return them to their bondage in Egypt."

- **Ellicott**: The verb for "dealt proudly" is the same Hebrew word used of the Egyptians in v. 10 (Ex. 18:11; Deut. 1:43) — Israel behaved just like their former oppressors. On "appointed a captain to return to their bondage," he notes: "This is the reading of some MSS., followed by the Septuagint, and is in harmony with Numbers 14:4, though there the appointment is only proposed." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Guzik (Enduring Word)**: "Our sin is bad enough; but to consider we sin against a God who has only treated us well is far, far, worse." This recognition of sinfulness is "a third sure sign of revival." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/

---

### v. 17b — The pivot: "But You are a forgiving God…"

"But You are a forgiving God, gracious and compassionate, slow to anger and rich in loving devotion, and You did not forsake them."

- **Ellicott**: "A God ready to pardon.—A God of pardons; only in Daniel 9:9 and Psalm 130:4." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Guzik**: "'Ready to pardon' is especially wonderful, indicating that there is nothing keeping God from pardoning us except our refusal to come to Him through Jesus. He is ready to pardon, if we are ready to receive it." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/
- **Spurgeon** preached a whole sermon on this phrase (Sermon No. 1272), referenced at: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/sbc/nehemiah-9.html

---

### v. 18 — The golden calf and "terrible blasphemies"

"Even when they cast for themselves an image of a calf and said, 'This is your God who brought you up out of Egypt.'"

- **Gill**: The calf was made "in imitation of the Apis, or ox of the Egyptians." The phrase "wrought great provocations" means "of all which nothing was greater than idolatry." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html

---

### vv. 19–21 — God's great compassion in the wilderness

"You in Your great compassion did not forsake them…You gave Your good Spirit to instruct them…For forty years You sustained them…they lacked nothing."

- **Gill**: On v. 19, if the pillar "had [departed], they would have been scorched by the heat of the sun." On v. 20, the "good spirit" is interpreted by some Jewish commentators (Ben Melech, Aben Ezra) as "the spirit of prophecy" given to the seventy elders (Num. 11:17). On v. 21, he cross-references Deut. 8:4. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "Thy good spirit.—Probably a reference to Numbers 11:17; Numbers 11:25. The epithet given to the Spirit is in Psalm 143:10. But His teaching function occurs here only, and is a remarkable anticipation of the New Testament." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm

**Denominational note (v. 20)**: The reference to "Your good Spirit to instruct them" is a key text for Pentecostal and charismatic traditions, which see here a foreshadowing of the Holy Spirit's teaching ministry in the believer's life. Ellicott's observation that "His teaching function occurs here only" highlights the uniqueness of this phrase in the OT. Pentecostal/charismatic commentators (e.g., those at Enduring Word / David Guzik) emphasize this as an anticipation of the NT promise that the Spirit would "teach you all things" (John 14:26).

- **Guzik**: Notes that God's gracious provision — the cloud, the fire, the Spirit, manna, water, preservation of clothes and feet — "together it all shows not how special Israel was, but how special God is." He adds, quoting Alan Redpath: "God's mercy with a sinner is only equaled and perhaps outmatched by His patience with the saints, with you and me." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/

---

### vv. 22–25 — The conquest and abundant blessing

"You gave them kingdoms and peoples…They captured fortified cities and fertile land…they ate and were filled; they grew fat and delighted in Your great goodness."

- **Gill**: The "kingdoms and nations" were Sihon, Og, and the seven nations of Canaan. "They took strong cities — such as, in an hyperbolical way, are said to be walled up to heaven (Deut. 1:28)." He notes the people "did eat, and were filled, and became fat; in body, though in mind became wanton and wicked." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html

---

### vv. 26–28 — The cycle: rebellion, oppression, deliverance, repeat

"They flung Your law behind their backs. They killed Your prophets…So You delivered them into the hands of enemies…they cried out to You. From heaven You heard them, and…gave them deliverers…But as soon as they had rest, they again did evil."

- **Gill**: "Cast thy law behind their backs — as of no account, and unworthy of their regard." The "saviours" or deliverers were the judges: Othniel, Ehud, Barak, Gideon, etc. This was "not on account of their merits, but the abundant unmerited mercy of the Lord." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Ellicott**: "The phraseology in this and the following verse shows that the Book of Judges is carefully remembered in the prayer." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Guzik**: "The cycle Israel experienced — blessing leading to pride, discipline bringing them back to God, temporary obedience followed by renewed rebellion — repeats throughout their history, yet God's mercy never changes or grows tired." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/
- **Derek Kidner (via Precept Austin)**: "Sin abounds, grace superabounds…. Throughout this miraculous pilgrimage 'they lacked nothing' (21) — and appreciated nothing (17)." — https://www.preceptaustin.org/nehemiah-9-commentary

---

### vv. 29–31 — God's patient admonition and continued mercy

"You admonished them to turn back to Your law…They stubbornly shrugged their shoulders…You were patient with them for many years…Yet they would not listen, so You gave them into the hands of the neighboring peoples. But in Your great compassion, You did not put an end to them."

- **Ellicott**: On v. 29, "which if a man do, he shall live in them" — this is the classic OT text (Lev. 18:5) that Paul wrestles with in Galatians 3:12 and Romans 10:5. He adds that "withdrew the shoulder" pictures oxen refusing the yoke. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Gill**: "Yet many years didst thou forbear them — throughout the reigns of several kings, such was God's longsuffering towards them: or, 'thou didst draw upon them'; that is, his mercy, as Jarchi interprets it; he drew it out of his heart, and prolonged it towards them." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html

**Reformed note (v. 29)**: The reference to "Your ordinances, by which a man will live if he practices them" (Lev. 18:5) is a significant text for Reformed covenant theology, which distinguishes between the law as a covenant of works (do this and live) and the covenant of grace. Reformed commentators on monergism.com note that this prayer as a whole demonstrates the impossibility of keeping the law meritoriously and drives the people back to God's mercy alone. — https://www.monergism.com/topics/sermon-manuscripts-mp3s-scripture/nehemiah/audio-multimedia/nehemiah-%E2%80%94-reformed-sermons-8

---

### v. 32 — The plea proper begins: "So now, our God, the great and mighty and awesome God"

- **Ellicott**: "Here begins the prayer proper." The reference to "the kings of Assyria" encompasses "Pul, Tiglath-pileser, Shalmaneser, Sargon, Sennacherib, Esar-haddon…as successive scourges." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Gill**: The titles (great, mighty, terrible, keeping covenant and mercy) are the same ones Nehemiah used in his personal prayer (Neh. 1:5), suggesting "the whole prayer is his composure, which was delivered by him to the Levites." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html

---

### v. 33 — "You are just…You have acted faithfully, while we have acted wickedly"

- **Gill**: "They own the justice of God, could not complain of any wrong done them; and had he shown them no mercy at all, it was but what they deserved." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/nehemiah-9.html
- **Guzik (quoting Alan Redpath)**: "It is a tremendous moment in a Christian's life when he can honestly look up into the face of God and say, 'Yes, Lord, You are right and I am wrong,' when he stops arguing with God, and drops his controversy. He says, 'Lord, yes. I've got what I deserved in this situation. You are right; I am wrong.' That is the thing for which God has been working in your life and mine from the very moment of our conversion." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/

---

### vv. 34–35 — Confession that kings, leaders, priests, and fathers did not obey

- **Ellicott**: On v. 34, "Our kings.—Note that the prophets are omitted in this enumeration" (contrast v. 32, where prophets were included in the list of those suffering). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm

---

### vv. 36–37 — The present distress: "Here we are today as slaves"

"So here we are today as slaves in the land You gave our fathers to enjoy…Its abundant harvest goes to the kings You have set over us because of our sins."

- **Ellicott**: "Yieldeth much increase.—In money and kind a very large amount was sent by Syria to the Persian treasury. Over our bodies, and over our cattle.—For military service; but the priests do not omit themselves." He notes the "pathetic comparison between the Divine purpose in giving the land originally and their present bondage in it extends almost to every word." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Guzik**: "In Nehemiah's day, Israel was not an independent nation — they were a province of the Persian Empire and were under heavy taxes and obligations." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/

---

### v. 38 — The binding agreement: a written and sealed covenant

"In view of all this, we make a binding agreement, putting it in writing and sealing it with the names of our leaders, Levites, and priests."

- **Ellicott**: "Because of all this.—On the ground of this confession, and to prove our sincerity. Seal unto it.—On the sealed [document]. Each party impressed his seal on moist clay, which was then hardened. Sometimes these seals were attached to the document by separate strings." — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/nehemiah/9.htm
- **Guzik**: "The fourth sure sign of revival — after brokenness of heart, after reflection on God's goodness, after recognition of our sinfulness, is a renewal of our obedience. We come to a place of decision, so this work of God is not just a wonderful experience, but something that shapes our future." — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/nehemiah-9/
- **Layman's Bible Commentary**: Notes that "the usual word for 'covenant' is lacking here." The verse serves as a transition to chapter 10, though some interpreters believe "it rather refers to some pledge of reform at another time." — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/nehemiah-9.html

---

### Key Protestant Distinctives Observable in This Chapter

1. **Reformed / Covenant Theology**: The entire prayer is a rehearsal of God's covenant faithfulness despite human unfaithfulness. Reformed readers see here the sovereignty of God in election (v. 7, God "chose Abram"), in preservation (v. 19–21), and in the "covenant and mercy" that God keeps (v. 32). The phrase "which if a man do, he shall live in them" (v. 29) is understood in Reformed theology as law that drives us to grace. — https://www.monergism.com/topics/sermon-manuscripts-mp3s-scripture/nehemiah/audio-multimedia/nehemiah-%E2%80%94-reformed-sermons-8

2. **Baptist**: The Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary emphasizes the pattern: "reading the word of God will convict one concerning his sin…the best thing for one convicted to do is to confess and seek God's forgiveness." It stresses personal application and the need for individual response. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/nehemiah-9.html

3. **Pentecostal / Charismatic**: v. 20 ("You gave Your good Spirit to instruct them") is a key text. Enduring Word (David Guzik, charismatic background) and Ellicott both note that the Spirit's teaching ministry is unique in the OT, and charismatic readers see here a type of the NT indwelling Spirit who teaches, guides, and instructs believers.

4. **Lutheran**: No specific Lutheran commentary on Nehemiah 9 was returned from the permitted sites (lcms.org, 1517.org). However, Lutheran theology would read the chapter through the lens of Law and Gospel: the Law read for three hours reveals sin; the confession and prayer for mercy reflects the Gospel of God's forgiving grace.

5. **Methodist / Holiness**: No specific Wesleyan commentary on this chapter was returned from the permitted sites. The Holiness tradition would emphasize the chapter's call to ongoing repentance, separation from worldliness (v. 2), and the renewal of obedience (v. 38) as evidence of sanctification.

---

### Other Views

For modern scholarship, Catholic, and Orthodox readings, no results were returned from the permitted sites (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) in the available searches. The Layman's Bible Commentary (via StudyLight) does reflect some critical scholarship in noting that the RSV "following the Greek translation, supplies the name of Ezra as the speaker" of the prayer from v. 6 onward, and that some interpreters see v. 38 as originally unconnected to the ceremony of ch. 9. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/nehemiah-9.html
